title: AI Governance
summary: AI governance is the set of policies, decision rights, controls and review processes an organisation uses to decide how artificial intelligence systems are proposed, approved, built, operated and retired. It spans the whole lifecycle rather than a single review: use case intake and risk classification, data sourcing and lawful basis, model evaluation and documentation, human oversight, monitoring for drift or harmful output, incident handling, and management of third party models and vendors. Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework are organised around functions for governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk rather than around a fixed checklist, so the practical work is translating those functions into your own approval gates, owners and retained evidence. Regulation adds reporting and transparency duties in some sectors and jurisdictions. The mistake people make is treating governance as a documentation exercise owned by legal: without technical controls, logging and a named owner for each deployed model, the policy cannot constrain anything at runtime.

beginner.definition: AI governance is the set of rules and roles that control how an organisation uses artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks we once thought only people could do. Governance decides who may build such a system, what data it may use and who checks it. It also says when a system must be switched off.
beginner.whyItMatters: A team can now add an AI feature in a few days. That speed means a risky system can reach customers before anybody reviews it. The model may use personal data it should not use. It may also give harmful advice to thousands of people at once. Clear rules and named owners stop those problems from hiding.
howItWorks: Someone proposes a new AI use case and describes what it will do.
A reviewer sorts the proposal by risk, such as the harm a wrong answer causes.
The team must show which data it will use and where that data came from.
Before release the system is tested for accuracy, fairness and possible misuse.
A named owner watches the system in production and records any problems.
The system is reviewed again on a schedule, or retired when it is no longer safe.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital that wants to buy a new scanning machine. A committee asks what it does, who operates it and what happens if it fails. They test it on the ward before anyone trusts it. One named person stays responsible for that machine for its whole life. AI governance is that committee, applied to software that learns.
takeaways: Every AI system needs a named owner who is accountable after release.
Decide the risk level before the build starts, not after the launch.
Keep evidence of tests, data sources and decisions so reviews are possible later.

objectives: Explain what AI governance covers across the lifecycle of an AI system.
Describe how use cases are classified by risk before development begins.
Identify the documentation and evidence a governance process should retain.
Explain the role of a named owner and of human oversight in production.
Describe how AI governance connects to existing risk and compliance work.
